Below is a non-exhaustive list of homophobic slurs, insults and pejorative phrases that have appeared in English-language discourse. They are presented solely for academic analysis of how negative language targets sexual orientation. All examples are offensive; inclusion here does not imply endorsement.

1. Single-word slurs (most severe)  
  • fag, faggot  
  • dyke  
  • tranny  
  • queer (used pejoratively)  
  • homo  
  • sissy  
  • fairy  
  • queeny  
  • lezbo  

2. Variants and compound insults  
  • fag-off, fagged, fagging (verb form)  
  • dykey, dykette  
  • trannie-fag  
  • queen-boy  
  • homo pervert, queer pervert  
  • cocksucking faggot  

3. Common derogatory phrases  
  • “That’s so gay.”  
  • “Are you gay or something?” (used as accusation)  
  • “No homo.”  
  • “Get back in the closet.”  
  • “Go find a parade.”  
  • “Adam and Eve, not Adam and Steve.”  

4. Extended insults and taunts  
  • “You’re such a little fairy.”  
  • “Stop prancing around like a queer.”  
  • “Only queers do that.”  
  • “Sick gay pervert.”  
  • “Stinky dyke.”  
  • “Worthless homo.”  

5. Derogatory humor/sarcasm  
  • “Did you catch any of those drag queens last night?” (implying mockery)  
  • “Oh, look—another lesbian bar.” (dismissive tone)  
  • “In your dreams, cupcake.” (often aimed at effeminate men)  

6. Contextual examples in speech or writing  
  –  “Don’t be such a fag.”  
  –  “I can’t stand those dykes.”  
  –  “He’s such a queen, always fussing over his hair.”  
  –  “What a homo thing to say.”  
  –  “Only a sissy would wear that.”  

Notes for academic use  
• Severity varies: single-word slurs (faggot, dyke, tranny) are highest in offensiveness; phrases like “that’s so gay” are widespread casual insults.  
• Many of these can be combined with intensifiers (“fucking fag,” “stupid dyke”) or used in rhetorical questions.  
• Some have been reclaimed by LGBT communities internally (queer, dyke) but remain highly offensive when used by outsiders.  
• Spelling variants (e.g. “fagette,” “trannygurl”) appear in online harassment.  
• When analyzing corpora, watch for euphemistic or coded language (e.g. “fruit,” “batty boy”) and emerging neo-slurs.  

Please handle this material with care: these terms perpetuate harm and stigma. Use contextual annotation (speaker identity, intended audience, co-occurring violence or threats) when assessing their impact.
